quoted_clause: (the §9.3 worked example's 40 GB/s and 2.5 GB/s are optimistic ~80% upper bounds — label them as such)
observed: This parenthetical reads as an editorial instruction to the author ('label them as such') rather than as content for the reader. It is embedded inside the first Common Mistakes bullet about peak vs sustained bandwidth.
evidence: The phrase 'label them as such' is an imperative directed at the author/editor. §9.3 already labels these values as assumptions ('an assumed effective two-rail 40 GB/s' and 'a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s'), making the instruction redundant as well as out of place in published prose.
root_cause: Editorial note left in manuscript during revision.
correction: Remove the parenthetical entirely, or rewrite it as reader-facing prose, e.g.: 'Note that the §9.3 worked example's 40 GB/s and 2.5 GB/s are optimistic ~80% upper bounds on effective bandwidth.'
acceptance_test: Search the manuscript for 'label them as such' and similar author-directed imperatives; none should appear in published text.

quoted_clause: A 70B model gradient all-reduce at 25 Gb/s Ethernet (≈ 2.5 GB/s practical-effective) takes ~56 s per step (a flat lower bound; ~98 s with the ring factor, §9.3).
observed: The main clause presents 56 s as the time the all-reduce 'takes,' but §9.3 explicitly states 56 s is the time for 'a one-way transfer of the logical 140 GB,' not for the all-reduce. The term 'flat lower bound' is never defined. For N=8 the ring all-reduce lower bound is 2(N−1)/N × M / B = 245/2.5 = 98 s; 56 s is achievable only with in-network reduction (e.g., SHARP), which is not available on standard Ethernet.
evidence: §9.3: 'A one-way transfer of the logical 140 GB alone would take 56 s at an assumed effective 2.5 GB/s; the ring's send volume instead gives 98 s.' The all-reduce data-movement lower bound for N=8 is 2(7/8)(140) = 245 GB per rank, giving 98 s at 2.5 GB/s. 56 s = 140/2.5 is the flat-transfer time, not an all-reduce lower bound on standard Ethernet.
root_cause: Conflation of flat-transfer time with all-reduce lower bound; 'flat' is undefined.
correction: Rephrase to: 'A flat one-way transfer of the 140 GB gradient takes ~56 s at 2.5 GB/s — a lower bound for any communication of this tensor. The ring all-reduce sends 245 GB per rank, giving ~98 s (§9.3).' Or define 'flat lower bound' explicitly as the in-network-reduction lower bound and note it is not achievable on standard Ethernet.
acceptance_test: The bullet should not present 56 s as the time the all-reduce 'takes' without immediately clarifying that it is a flat-transfer lower bound, not an achievable all-reduce time on Ethernet.

quoted_clause: InfiniBand HDR/NDR | 200/400 Gb/s ≈ 25/50 GB/s per port | ~us | high capex | [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
observed: The row-level [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] tag applies to the entire row per the table note ('except where a row is tagged otherwise'). This incorrectly implies the 200/400 Gb/s bandwidth specification is illustrative when it is an established InfiniBand Trade Association specification ([1P][FACT]). The derived GB/s conversion (≈ 25/50) is correctly [DERIVED], and the latency (~us) and cost (high capex) are correctly [ILLUSTRATIVE], but the raw Gb/s spec is mislabeled.
evidence: HDR = 200 Gb/s and NDR = 400 Gb/s per port are defined in the IBTA InfiniBand specification — first-party specs, not illustrative estimates. The table note says bandwidth figures default to [1P][FACT] 'except where a row is tagged otherwise,' so the row tag overrides the correct default for the bandwidth column.
root_cause: Row-level label is too coarse to distinguish spec-level bandwidth from illustrative latency/cost within the same row.
correction: Either split the label per column (bandwidth: [1P][FACT][DERIVED]; latency: [ILLUSTRATIVE]; cost: [ILLUSTRATIVE]) or add a footnote to the InfiniBand row clarifying that the Gb/s figures are IBTA specifications while the latency and cost are illustrative.
acceptance_test: The InfiniBand bandwidth (200/400 Gb/s) should be identifiable as [1P][FACT] from the table alone, consistent with the table note's default.

page_hint: Section 5, Common Mistakes, fifth bullet (protocol overhead)
quoted_clause: 200/400GbE transcodes 64b/66b to 256b/257b before FEC
observed: The claim that 200/400GbE 'transcodes 64b/66b to 256b/257b before FEC' needs verification against IEEE 802.3. The PCS layer for 200GBASE-R/400GBASE-R uses 64b/66b encoding; the subsequent FEC (typically RS(544,514) / KP4) operates on different block structures. The phrase 'transcodes to 256b/257b' implies a direct encoding conversion that may not accurately describe the standard's layering. Additionally, 200GbE and 400GbE may use different lane counts and FEC configurations, making the lumped '200/400GbE' claim potentially imprecise.
evidence: IEEE 802.3 clauses for 200GBASE-R and 400GBASE-R specify 64b/66b at the PCS layer. The KP4 FEC (RS(544,514)) uses a different block structure. The specific relationship between 64b/66b and any 256b/257b encoding in the FEC path needs primary-source verification. The claim is tagged [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] which provides some scope, but the mechanism description should be accurate even if illustrative.
root_cause: Encoding-layer description may be a simplification or may conflate gearbox/FEC block sizes with a distinct encoding scheme.
correction: Verify against IEEE 802.3 clauses for 200GBASE-R/400GBASE-R. If the 256b/257b reference is to a specific gearbox or FEC block size, rephrase to name the correct layer (e.g., 'the PCS uses 64b/66b; the KP4 FEC operates on 256-bit blocks'). If uncertain, simplify to: 'use the specific standard's payload-efficiency figure' without the specific encoding claim.
acceptance_test: The encoding claim should be verifiable against a specific IEEE 802.3 clause, or be removed/simplified.

quoted_clause: the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs, at the canonical batch and hidden size — it scales with batch × hidden width per layer)
observed: The parenthetical '(tens of MBs...)' is ambiguous: it could refer to each per-layer all-reduce or to the per-step total across all layers. For a 70B model with hidden_size ≈ 8192, batch 32, FP16, each per-layer activation all-reduce is ~512 KB (sub-MB), while the per-step total across ~80 layers is ~40 MB (tens of MBs). The phrase 'it scales with batch × hidden width per layer' suggests the per-step total, but the proximity to 'per-layer activations' invites the per-layer reading.
evidence: Per-layer activation for decode: batch × hidden_size × 2 bytes = 32 × 8192 × 2 = 524,288 bytes ≈ 512 KB. Per-step total across ~80 layers: 80 × 512 KB ≈ 40 MB. 'Tens of MBs' matches the per-step total, not the per-layer figure.
root_cause: Ambiguous referent for the quantity in parentheses.
correction: Rephrase to: 'the per-step total across all layers is tens of MBs (each individual per-layer all-reduce is sub-MB at the canonical batch and hidden size).'
acceptance_test: A reader should be able to determine from the sentence alone whether 'tens of MBs' refers to per-layer or per-step total.

page_hint: Ch 11 §3 Worked Example, 'Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU' bullet 1
quoted_clause: inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach
observed: The canonical workload (same section, two paragraphs earlier) defines 'TTFT budget 1.2 s'. The discrete-batching discussion then says TTFT inflates 'toward the 2 s SLO breach'. The relationship between the 1.2 s budget and the 2 s breach is never explained. A reader cannot tell whether the TTFT SLO is 1.2 s or 2 s, whether 2 s is a hard limit vs. a soft budget, or whether 2 s refers to a different metric entirely.
evidence: Direct textual comparison within the same section: 'TTFT budget 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms/token. [ASSUMPTION]' vs. 'inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach.' No intervening text defines a 2 s TTFT threshold or explains a budget-vs-SLO distinction.
root_cause: Either the canonical TTFT SLO is 1.2 s (making '2 s' an error), or there is an unstated two-tier budget/hard-limit structure, or '2 s' refers to end-to-end latency (but the clause explicitly says TTFT).
correction: If the TTFT SLO is 1.2 s, change '2 s' to '1.2 s'. If there is a two-tier structure (1.2 s target, 2 s hard limit), add a one-clause explanation at first use. If 2 s is end-to-end, rewrite to say so explicitly.
acceptance_test: After the fix, a reader can state the TTFT SLO and the TTFT breach threshold (if different) without ambiguity, and both numbers are consistent with the canonical workload definition in Ch 4.

quoted_clause: Replicates: model + optimizer | Communicates: gradients → all-reduce (per step)
observed: The DP row in Table 10-1 describes only training DP (replicates optimizer, all-reduces gradients). The chapter text (§1, §2, §3, §6) explicitly and repeatedly distinguishes training DP from inference DP (independent replicas, no gradient sync, no optimizer). The table does not note this distinction, so a reader who consults the table alone will form an incorrect model of inference DP.
evidence: Table 10-1 DP row: 'Replicates: model + optimizer; Communicates: gradients → all-reduce (per step)'. Chapter text §1: 'In inference, DP simply means running independent model replicas to raise throughput — there is no gradient sync at all.' §6: 'Gradient synchronization applies only to training or fine-tuning.'
root_cause: The table was written for training DP and not updated when the chapter added the training/inference distinction.
correction: Either (a) add a footnote to the DP row: 'Training DP; inference DP replicates the model only and communicates nothing (independent replicas)', or (b) split the row into 'DP (training)' and 'DP (inference)', or (c) change the Replicates cell to 'model (+ optimizer in training)' and the Communicates cell to 'gradients → all-reduce (training only; inference: none)'.
acceptance_test: A reader who reads only Table 10-1 can correctly state what inference DP replicates and communicates.

quoted_clause: Communicates: KV → ring
observed: The CP row specifies 'ring' as the communication pattern, but the chapter text (§1 item 5) only says CP 'splits the sequence dimension across GPUs' and never establishes a ring collective for CP. Ring is one possible implementation; Megatron-style sequence parallelism typically uses all-gather/reduce-scatter, and inference KV sharding can use various patterns. Introducing 'ring' in the table without textual support is an unsupported specificity.
evidence: §1 item 5: 'Sequence/context parallelism (CP) splits the sequence dimension across GPUs' — no mention of ring. Table 10-1 CP row: 'Communicates: KV → ring'. No other location in the chunk establishes ring for CP.
root_cause: The table cell was filled with a specific collective name that the prose does not establish or justify for CP.
correction: Change to a general description such as 'KV → sequence collectives (all-gather / reduce-scatter / ring, implementation-dependent)' or simply 'KV → sequence-dimension collectives', matching the level of specificity used for other rows.
acceptance_test: The CP row's Communicates cell uses a term that is either defined in the chapter text or explicitly marked as implementation-dependent.

quoted_clause: the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point
observed: The number 17.5 appears as 'the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point' with no cross-reference to where it is established. The reader cannot verify this number from the current chapter. It is used to compute decode arithmetic intensity (AI = B ≈ 17.5) and to argue that decode is bandwidth-bound, so its provenance matters.
evidence: The clause appears in Ch 11 §3 without a chapter/section reference. The canonical workload definition in the same section lists rps, tokens, TTFT, and TPOT but not concurrency = 17.5. Memory-based estimate (500 GB / 24.1 GB ≈ 20.7) and Little's Law (10 × 7.5 = 75) both differ from 17.5.
root_cause: The number is presumably established in Ch 6 or another earlier chapter but the cross-reference was omitted.
correction: Add a cross-reference at first use: 'the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point (Ch X, §Y)' or briefly state how 17.5 is derived (e.g., 'the decode batch size at the canonical operating point, Ch 6').
acceptance_test: A reader can locate the derivation or definition of 17.5 without leaving the book, and the number is consistent with its use in the arithmetic-intensity argument.

quoted_clause: §1: 'up to 525% throughput lift' vs §3: 'up to 525% long-context throughput (a lift over the paper's own baseline configuration…)'
observed: §1 says '525% throughput lift' (unambiguously an improvement of 525%, i.e., 6.25× baseline). §3 says '525% long-context throughput' which could be read as 525% of baseline (5.25×) before the parenthetical clarifies it as a lift. The two phrasings are not identical and the second is momentarily ambiguous.
evidence: Direct textual comparison of the two occurrences within the same chapter.
root_cause: Inconsistent phrasing between the concept list and the worked example.
correction: Unify the phrasing. Either both say '525% throughput lift' or both say 'up to 6.25× throughput (a 525% lift over baseline)'. The §3 parenthetical is good; make §1 equally explicit.
acceptance_test: Both occurrences use the same unambiguous construction, and a reader cannot momentarily misread 525% as '525% of baseline'.

quoted_clause: The team's 'parallelism is slow' becomes a precise, diagnosed, and fixed split.
observed: The mini-case describes the architect's reasoning process (measure residency, choose PP/EP/TP, measure interconnect, choose P and m) but never shows a concrete symptom (e.g., 'TPOT is 80 ms'), a concrete measurement (e.g., 'inter-node all-reduce takes 15 ms per layer'), or a concrete before/after comparison. The closing claim that the problem is 'diagnosed and fixed' is asserted, not demonstrated.
evidence: The mini-case contains no measured or illustrative numbers for the symptom, the bottleneck, or the improvement. The only numbers are the 800 GB weight estimate and the ~40B active assumption.
root_cause: The mini-case was written as a narrative walkthrough rather than a problem-solving exercise with evidence.
correction: Add at least one concrete symptom (e.g., 'TPOT measured at 80 ms vs. 25 ms target'), one measurement that reveals the bottleneck (e.g., 'inter-node all-reduce accounts for 45 ms of the 80 ms'), and one before/after number showing the fix (e.g., 'switching from cross-node TP to PP reduced TPOT to 35 ms'). This transforms the mini-case from a summary into a transferable reasoning exercise.
acceptance_test: The mini-case contains at least one specific measured or illustrative number for the symptom, one for the diagnosed bottleneck, and one for the post-fix result, and the reader can trace the causal chain from symptom to fix.

page_hint: Ch 11 §4 'Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability' through end of chapter
quoted_clause: A hybrid model (a transformer interleaved with a recurrent/state-space block) can require both paged history and bounded recurrent state.
observed: The 'Serving qualification' subsection (followed by adaptive-depth and economic-denominator paragraphs) covers hybrid models, looped-depth models, early-exit interfaces, adaptive-depth batching, depth-distribution latency evaluation, and economic denominators. These are specialized topics that go well beyond the chapter's core four mechanisms (continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix caching, P/D disaggregation). The subsection is ~5 paragraphs long and introduces several new concepts (looped-depth, adaptive depth, early-exit head) that are not used elsewhere in the chapter.
evidence: The chapter's stated scope (§ Architect's Question) is 'how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode.' The Serving qualification subsection addresses none of these four topics directly.
root_cause: Material that belongs to a model-selection or advanced-serving chapter was placed here, possibly because it was written during a serving-engine discussion.
correction: Either (a) move the subsection to a later chapter on model selection / advanced serving, (b) condense it to 1–2 paragraphs focused on the key point ('model support ≠ serving capability; verify state representation, cache policy, and execution paths before assuming an engine supports a model'), or (c) keep it but add a framing sentence explaining why it appears here (e.g., 'Before choosing a serving engine, verify that it supports the model's state requirements — a point that becomes critical when…').
acceptance_test: The subsection either appears in a chapter whose scope includes model-engine compatibility, or is condensed to directly support one of the chapter's four core mechanisms, or has an explicit framing sentence connecting it to the chapter's argument.

quoted_clause: Communication-specificity note: the TP collective is algorithm-dependent — a plain all-reduce of partial sums is one option, but fused kernels often use reduce-scatter + all-gather (or a single all-reduce) depending on the framework; the PP bubble size depends on microbatch scheduling (more microbatches shrink the bubble but add memory). The panels show the canonical configuration (TP all-reduce per layer; PP with a small fixed microbatch count; GPU counts and layer ranges schematic — the canonical host is 8×H100 and the canonical 70B has 80 layers); substitute the actual collective and schedule for the target stack. Grayscale note: each box's text label carries its role, so the in-figure color key (blue = weights · orange = GPU · green = data · red = comms) is redundant, not load-bearing.
observed: The caption is extremely long (~150 words) and contains three distinct layers of commentary: (1) a description of the three panels, (2) a communication-specificity note about TP collectives and PP microbatch scheduling, and (3) a grayscale accessibility note. The communication-specificity note is substantive content that belongs in the prose, not the caption. The grayscale note is a production note that belongs in a figure note or the production spec.
evidence: Caption word count and content layering. The prose immediately after the figure already restates the three patterns, so the caption's communication-specificity note duplicates prose content while also being too long for a caption.
root_cause: Accumulated editorial notes were appended to the caption rather than placed in the appropriate location (prose, figure note, or production spec).
correction: Move the communication-specificity note to the prose paragraph immediately after the figure (where the three patterns are already described). Move the grayscale note to a figure note below the caption or to the production spec. Keep the caption to a concise description of what the three panels show plus the [ILLUSTRATIVE] label.
acceptance_test: The caption is under ~60 words, describes what the reader should learn from the figure, and does not contain production notes or substantive technical commentary that belongs in prose.

page_hint: Ch 10 §2, Table 10-1, Data (DP) row, 'Fits when' column

observed: The 'Fits when' cell for DP contains a ~30-word parenthetical explanation that is too long for a table cell. It disrupts the table's visual rhythm and makes the cell hard to scan. The same information appears in the chapter prose (§3 Worked Example).
evidence: Table cell word count vs. other cells in the same column (all other cells are 3–8 words).
root_cause: Explanatory prose was placed in a table cell instead of a footnote or the body text.

page_hint: Ch 10 §7 'What We Still Don't Know', bullet 2
quoted_clause: 2026 MoE scaling has moved the specialist/EP frontier. Kimi K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE [1P: arXiv 2607.24653]; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next routes 10+1 of 512 experts (125B total / 6B active) [1P: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next].
observed: This bullet presents specific model architecture facts (expert counts, activation ratios, parameter totals) as if they were open questions. The section is titled 'What We Still Don't Know,' but the bullet states things that are known (the model specs) rather than things that are unknown. The implicit open question — 'how should architects size EP for models at this sparsity level?' — is never explicitly stated.
evidence: The bullet's content is factual (model specifications with [1P] citations), not uncertain. Compare with the other bullets in the section, which correctly identify genuine uncertainties (optimal split, communication-overlap efficiency, P/D parallelism choice).
root_cause: Observational context was placed in an open-questions section without being reframed as a question.
correction: Reframe as an explicit open question: 'How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE models with extreme sparsity (e.g., Kimi K3's 16/896 ≈ 1.8% activation, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 10+1/512)? The activated footprint (104B / 6B) drives compute, but total residency (2.8T / 125B) drives EP sharding — the crossover between these two constraints at current interconnect bandwidths is unmeasured [UNRESOLVED].' Or move the factual model specs to a sidebar in §1 or §3.
acceptance_test: Every bullet in 'What We Still Don't Know' states an explicit uncertainty (with an appropriate label), not a known fact.

page_hint: Ch 10 §6 Architecture Consequence, 'The canonical answer' bullet
quoted_clause: Eight ranks are the chosen baseline, not a minimum derived from weight bytes alone.
observed: The text correctly notes that TP=8 is a choice rather than a weight-bytes minimum (TP=2 would suffice for 140 GB / 2 = 70 GB < 80 GB), but never explains why 8 was chosen. The reader is told what TP=8 is not (a minimum) but not what it is (a throughput/latency/topology choice).
evidence: The sentence acknowledges the gap ('not a minimum derived from weight bytes alone') but provides no positive rationale. Earlier in the chapter, TP=2 is shown to be sufficient for weights.
root_cause: The author flagged the distinction but did not follow through with the explanation.
correction: Add a brief rationale: 'Eight ranks are the chosen baseline, not a minimum derived from weight bytes alone — TP=2 would hold the weights, but TP=8 matches the node's 8-GPU topology, keeps per-rank weight reads well within HBM bandwidth (0.7 TB/s vs. 3.35 TB/s peak), and leaves headroom for KV and activations.'
acceptance_test: The reader can state at least one positive reason for choosing TP=8 over TP=2 for the canonical host.

quoted_clause: §1 first: 'These are not alternatives; production systems compose them (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within a node × PP across a few nodes…)' vs §1 second: 'The three primary patterns compose (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within a node × PP across a few nodes) — which dimension binds determines which to split first.'
observed: The composition point and the same example (DP × TP × PP) appear twice within §1, separated only by the figure and its prose description. The second occurrence adds 'which dimension binds determines which to split first' but otherwise restates the first.
evidence: Direct textual comparison within the same section.
root_cause: The figure prose paragraph restated a point already made before the figure.
correction: In the post-figure prose, keep only the new insight ('which dimension binds determines which to split first') and drop the repeated composition example, or merge the two into one occurrence.
acceptance_test: The composition point and its example appear once in §1; the post-figure prose adds only new content.

quoted_clause: 2 × 70 × 10⁹ × 8,000 ≈ 1.12 PFLOP — the book's K = 1,000, since 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200; the full 9.2K canonical input is ~1.29 PFLOP
observed: The K = 1,000 house-convention reminder is embedded in the middle of a FLOP calculation, disrupting the arithmetic flow. The reader is following a numerical derivation and is interrupted by a definitional aside.

quoted_clause: 'the canonical 8×H100 host (640 GB total)' / 'the canonical host is 8×H100 and the canonical 70B has 80 layers' / 'the canonical 70B/8×H100 baseline uses intra-host TP=8'
observed: The canonical configuration (70B, 8×H100, 640 GB, 80 layers) is restated in full at multiple points within the chapter. Each restatement is individually correct, but the cumulative effect is mild redundancy.
evidence: At least three full restatements of the canonical configuration within Ch 10.

page_hint: Ch 12 §8 Mini-Case, paragraph beginning "The consequence must be stated"
quoted_clause: ~$232.2K self-host and ~$467.2K cloud-equivalent at the same per-host rates ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis, Ch 16
observed: The 32-host self-host cost is stated as ~$232.2K, but proportional scaling from the stated 21-host cost gives 32/21 × $155,816.93 = $237,435 ≈ $237.4K. The cloud figure ($467.2K = 32/21 × $306,600 = $467,200) is correct, confirming the per-host-rate scaling method. The self-host figure is off by ~$5,235 (2.2%).
evidence: 32/21 × $155,816.93 = $237,435.20. Per-host: $155,816.93/21 = $7,419.85; 32 × $7,419.85 = $237,435.20. The stated $232,200 implies a per-host rate of $7,256.25, which contradicts "at the same per-host rates."
root_cause: Arithmetic error in scaling the 21-host self-host cost to 32 hosts; possibly a stale intermediate value or a different per-host rate used without disclosure.
correction: Replace ~$232.2K with ~$237.4K (or recompute from the authoritative per-host rate if a different basis is intended and state it).
acceptance_test: 32/21 × $155,816.93 ≈ $237.4K; the printed figure must match within rounding tolerance.

page_hint: Ch 12 §7 What We Still Don't Know, third bullet
quoted_clause: P/D-disaggregation communication overhead in multi-host settings. The boundary between parameter-parallel and data-parallel placement is relatively unexplored at the 70B scale
observed: The bullet is titled about P/D disaggregation communication overhead (KV transfer between prefill and decode pools), but the body discusses "the boundary between parameter-parallel and data-parallel placement," which is a different architectural dimension (how the model is sharded within a pool vs. how requests are replicated across pools). P/D disaggregation is orthogonal to TP/PP vs. DP placement.
evidence: P/D disaggregation splits computation by phase (prefill vs. decode) and transfers KV state between pools. Parameter-parallel (TP/PP) splits model weights; data-parallel (DP) replicates the model. These are independent axes. The open question conflates them.
root_cause: Conceptual confusion between the P/D disaggregation axis and the model-parallelism axis when writing the open question.
correction: Rewrite the bullet to address the actual open question: KV-transfer volume and latency between prefill and decode pools as a function of context length, request rate, and fabric bandwidth — or retitle it to match the parameter/data-parallel content if that is the intended question.
acceptance_test: The bullet's title and body address the same architectural concern; P/D disaggregation and TP/PP/DP are not conflated.

page_hint: Ch 11 §6 Architecture Consequence, italic paragraph after Fig 11.3; also Note 11.3-1
quoted_clause: prefill needs compute capacity (~1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 peak single-H100)
observed: The 1.19 PFLOPS figure equals 1.288 PFLOP (9,200 × 140 GFLOP/token) ÷ 1.08 s, but the 1.08 s prefill time is not derived anywhere in the chunk. At the book's standard 35% MFU on 8×H100, one request's prefill takes 1.288/2.77 = 0.465 s, not 1.08 s. The 1.08 s figure corresponds to ~15% MFU or to ~2.3 requests sharing the GPU — neither assumption is stated. The comparison "1.19 PFLOPS vs 0.989 peak single-H100" is also ambiguous: a reader may read it as the workload's aggregate requirement (which is 12.88 PFLOPS) rather than a per-request rate.
evidence: 9,200 × 140 GFLOP = 1.288 PFLOP. 1.288/1.08 = 1.19 PFLOPS. At 35% MFU on 8×H100: 8 × 989 × 0.35 = 2,769 GFLOPS = 2.77 PFLOPS; 1.288/2.77 = 0.465 s. The 1.08 s figure matches 15% MFU (1.288/1.187 = 1.085 s) or 2.32 concurrent prefill requests at 35% MFU.
root_cause: The 1.08 s prefill time (and derived 1.19 PFLOPS) uses an unstated assumption about concurrency or MFU that differs from the book's standard 35% MFU single-request basis.
correction: Either (a) derive the 1.08 s figure explicitly (state the concurrency or effective MFU assumption), or (b) replace with the 35% MFU figure (0.465 s per request, 2.77 PFLOPS aggregate on 8×H100) and compare against 8×H100's peak rather than a single H100's peak. Clarify whether 1.19 PFLOPS is a per-request rate or an aggregate requirement.
acceptance_test: The prefill time and PFLOPS figure can be reproduced from stated assumptions (MFU, concurrency, context length) using the book's own FLOP estimate (140 GFLOP/token for 70B).

page_hint: Ch 11 §6 Architecture Consequence, italic paragraph after Fig 11.3
quoted_clause: the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host
observed: The 5.6 TB/s figure equals 140 GB × 40 tokens/s (unbatched, batch size 1, at 25 ms TPOT), and 0.70 TB/s equals 17.5 GB × 40 tokens/s per GPU. Neither the batch size (1) nor the decode rate (40 tokens/s = 1/25 ms) is stated. A reader may misinterpret 5.6 TB/s as the batched aggregate rate or as the achieved rate rather than the unbatched required rate.
evidence: 140 GB × 40 = 5,600 GB/s = 5.6 TB/s. 17.5 GB × 40 = 700 GB/s = 0.70 TB/s. 40 tokens/s = 1/0.025 s (25 ms TPOT). With batch size B, the weight-read rate is 140 × 40/B GB/s, which is lower.
root_cause: The batch-size-1 assumption and the 40 tokens/s decode rate are implicit, not stated.
correction: State the assumptions: "at batch size 1 and 25 ms TPOT (40 tokens/s), the unbatched weight-read rate is 140 GB × 40 = 5.6 TB/s…" and note that batching reduces this proportionally.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 5.6 TB/s and 0.70 TB/s from stated assumptions (model size, TPOT, batch size, GPU count).

quoted_clause: Only the finalists — Candidates (a) and (b) — carry forward into the evaluation chapters (Chs. 14–16) with distinct test plans (Candidate (c) does not advance as a finalist; it is carried only as a labeled sensitivity case)
observed: The sentence says "Only the finalists — (a) and (b) — carry forward" but the parenthetical immediately says (c) "is carried" as a sensitivity case, and the following sentences describe evaluating (c) on quality-degradation trade-off. If (c) is carried, then "only the finalists carry forward" is false as stated.
evidence: Direct contradiction within the same sentence: "Only (a) and (b) carry forward" vs. "(c) is carried as a sensitivity case."
root_cause: The word "Only" overstates the exclusion; (c) is carried forward but in a different role.
correction: Rewrite: "Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as finalists into the evaluation chapters (Chs. 14–16) with distinct test plans. Candidate (c) is carried as a labeled sensitivity case, not a finalist."
acceptance_test: The sentence does not simultaneously claim "only (a) and (b) carry forward" and "(c) is carried."

quoted_clause: Serving is four separable concerns, not a stack (they interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency — but each is chosen independently)
observed: The caption asserts both "separable" / "chosen independently" and "they interact." The figure spec describes a flow (request stream → scheduler → KV page table → optional P/D split → output), which implies sequential dependency, not four independent dials. The tension between "separable" and "flow" may confuse readers about whether the four concerns can truly be chosen independently.
evidence: Caption says "separable" and "chosen independently" but also "they interact." Figure spec says "mechanism-first serving-flow diagram" with arrows connecting stages — a flow, not four independent boxes.
root_cause: The caption tries to convey both independence and interaction but the wording creates a contradiction; the figure spec (flow) reinforces the interaction reading.
correction: Clarify the intended claim: e.g., "four concerns that can be addressed in any order, though they interact (batching pressure feeds KV residency)" — or restructure the figure to show four parallel dials if independence is the primary message.
acceptance_test: The caption's claim about separability/independence is consistent with the figure's visual structure (flow vs. parallel dials).

quoted_clause: the KV-cache footprint must fit the target host's aggregate memory
observed: "KV-cache" (hyphenated) appears as a compound modifier here, while "KV cache" (unhyphenated) is used throughout the rest of the chunk (e.g., Ch 11, Ch 12 §3, Ch 13, Ch 14).
evidence: Ch 12 §1: "KV-cache footprint"; Ch 12 §3: "KV cache for 9.2K context"; Ch 13: "KV for the 9.5K max context"; Ch 14: "KV cache utilization."
root_cause: Inconsistent hyphenation of a compound modifier.
correction: Standardize to "KV cache" (unhyphenated) throughout, or consistently hyphenate when used as a compound modifier before a noun.
acceptance_test: Global search for "KV-cache" returns only intentional compound-modifier uses, or zero if unhyphenated form is canonical.

quoted_clause: The KV-transfer arrow is the load-bearing cost — it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB for the 13.3K-token context of §9.8; the canonical 9.2K-token request carries ~24.1 GB) across the joining link, so disaggregation pays only when the specialization benefit exceeds that transfer plus routing overhead. Caveat: see the in-figure aggregate-KV caveat (per-request times assume an unshared per-GPU link).
observed: The caption is very long (~80 words of dense numerical detail) and substantially duplicates Note 11.3-1, which appears immediately below the figure. Figure captions should orient the reader to what to look at; the detailed derivation belongs in the note/prose.
evidence: Caption contains ~35 GB, 13.3K tokens, 24.1 GB, 9.2K tokens, aggregate-KV caveat — all repeated in Note 11.3-1 with full derivation.
root_cause: Caption was used as a container for numerical detail rather than as a figure orientation aid.
correction: Shorten the caption to the figure's purpose and key takeaway (e.g., "P/D disaggregation has two cases: within-NVLink and cross-host; the KV-transfer cost decides whether it pays — see Note 11.3-1 for derivation"). Move numerical detail to the note.
acceptance_test: Caption is under ~40 words and does not duplicate Note 11.3-1's numerical derivations.

quoted_clause: a single card sustains ~24,700 prefill tokens/s (989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token = 24,725
observed: The same figure is written as "~24,700" in the prose and "24,725" in the parenthetical derivation. The rounding is inconsistent within the same sentence.
root_cause: Prose rounds to 3 significant figures while the derivation shows the exact value.
correction: Use one form consistently: either "~24,700 (24,725 exact)" or just "24,725" in both places.
acceptance_test: The same quantity uses consistent rounding within a single sentence.
